title: Python Basics: Numbers, Text & Operators
sub: Values, types, strings, bytes and the operators that connect them, with a reference card for every built-in and string method
goals: Choose the right numeric type and predict the result of //, %, ** and rounding
Slice, search and format strings, including the f-string format-spec mini-language
Convert between str and bytes and explain what an encoding does
Use comparison, logical, bitwise, membership and identity operators and know their precedence
Apply an IP mask with bitwise operators and convert values safely between types

blocks.text: Every program is values and operations on values. In this chapter you will learn Python's core value types (numbers, booleans, `None`, text and raw bytes), the operators that combine them, and the reference tools you will keep reopening: a card for each built-in function and each string method. The running theme is networking data: addresses as integers, masks as bit patterns, MAC addresses as hex strings, protocol text as bytes.
Every `run` block below is editable. Change a number, predict the output before pressing Run, and check yourself. The habit "predict, run, compare" teaches faster than rereading.
Numbers
Python has three numeric types you will use: `int` (whole numbers), `float` (decimals) and, rarely, `complex`. Their behavior is the base of everything else.

blocks.code:
print(type(7), type(7.0), type(3 + 4j))
print(2 ** 64)               # int never overflows
print(1_000_000 + 0xFF + 0b1010 + 0o17)
print(int.bit_length(255), (255).bit_length(), (256).bit_length())
print(7 / 2, 7 // 2, 7 % 2)
print(-7 // 2, -7 % 2)       # floor division rounds toward negative infinity

items.text: **`int`** has unlimited size, so `2 ** 64` and `3 ** 200` are exact. Literals can use `_` for readability (`1_000_000`) and prefixes `0x` (hex), `0b` (binary) and `0o` (octal). All of those are the same type: the base is only how you write it.

**`/`** always returns a `float`. **`//`** divides and rounds *down* toward negative infinity (so `-7 // 2` is `-4`). **`%`** is the remainder and takes the sign of the right operand. The two always agree: `a == (a // b) * b + a % b`.
**Power** (the double star) groups right to left, so `2 ** 3 ** 2` is `2 ** 9`, and `-2 ** 2` is `-4` because the power binds tighter than the minus sign.

blocks.text: Floats are binary fractions
A `float` is a 64-bit IEEE 754 value: 53 significant bits, about 15 to 17 decimal digits. Most decimal fractions have no exact binary form, which produces the famous surprises:

blocks.code:
print(0.1 + 0.2)
print(0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3)
import math
print(math.isclose(0.1 + 0.2, 0.3))
print(round(2.5), round(3.5), round(2.675, 2))
print(float("inf") > 10 ** 308, float("nan") == float("nan"))

blocks.text: Three rules follow. Never test floats with `==`; use `math.isclose`. `round` uses **banker's rounding** (ties go to the even neighbour: `round(2.5)` is `2`), and `round(2.675, 2)` gives `2.67` because the stored value is slightly below 2.675. `nan` (not a number) is not equal to anything, including itself. When exact decimal arithmetic matters, such as money, use the standard-library `decimal` module; for exact fractions use `fractions`.

blocks.code:
from decimal import Decimal
from fractions import Fraction
print(Decimal("0.1") + Decimal("0.2"))
print(Fraction(1, 3) + Fraction(1, 6))

blocks.text: bool and None

`bool` has exactly two values, `True` and `False`, and it is a subclass of `int`: `True + True` is `2`. `None` is the single "no value" object, with its own type `NoneType`. A function that does not `return` anything returns `None`. Test for it with `is None`, never `== None`.

blocks.code:
print(True + True, isinstance(True, int))
def nothing():
    pass
print(nothing(), nothing() is None)

blocks.text: Truthiness
Anywhere Python needs a yes/no answer (`if`, `while`, `and`, `or`, `not`) it converts the value with `bool()`. The **falsy** values are few and worth memorising; everything else is truthy.

blocks.code:
for value in [0, 1, "", "0", "False", [], [0], None, 0.0, 0.1]:
    print(repr(value), bool(value))
blocks.out:
0 False
1 True
'' False
'0' True
'False' True
[] False
[0] True
None False
0.0 False
0.1 True

blocks.text: `bool("False")` is `True`, because any non-empty string is truthy. When you read a flag from a file or the command line, compare the text: `value.lower() in ("1", "true", "yes")`.
Strings
A `str` is an immutable sequence of Unicode characters. Quote it with `'single'` or `"double"` (identical), or with `"""triple quotes"""` for several lines. Backslash starts an **escape**.
A **raw string** (`r"..."`) leaves backslashes alone, which is what you want for regular expressions and Windows-style paths. Compare:

blocks.code:
print("C:\new\table")
print(r"C:\new\table")
print("tab:[\t] newline-escape-count:", "a\nb".count("\n"))
poem = """line one
line two"""
print(poem.splitlines())
blocks.out:
C:
ew	able
C:\new\table
tab:[	] newline-escape-count: 1
['line one', 'line two']

blocks.text: Indexing and slicing

Strings are sequences, so every character has a position starting at 0, and negative positions count from the end. A **slice** `s[start:stop:step]` takes characters from `start` up to but not including `stop`; any part may be omitted.

blocks.code:
s = "ROUTER"
          R    O    U    T    E    R
          0    1    2    3    4    5        positive index
         -6   -5   -4   -3   -2   -1        negative index

   s[1:4]  → "OUT"      s[:3]  → "ROU"      s[-2:] → "ER"
   s[::2]  → "RUE"      s[::-1] → "RETUOR"  s[10:] → ""   (out of range slices are safe)

blocks.out:
R R OUT ROU ER RUE RETUOR
192 10
12 True 192.168.1.10/24 ------------

tokens.exp: the string being sliced, then the opening bracket
start omitted (0) up to, but not including, the position of the first dot
the slice ends; here it returns "192"

blocks.text: A single index outside the string raises `IndexError`, but a slice never does. Because strings are **immutable**, you cannot assign to a position (`s[0] = "r"` is a `TypeError`); you build a new string instead.

blocks.code:
s = "router"
s[0] = "R"

blocks.text: f-strings and the format-spec mini-language

An **f-string** is a string literal with an `f` prefix. Inside `{ }` you can put any expression, optionally followed by `!r` (use `repr`) and `:spec` (how to format). It is the default way to build text in modern Python.

tokens.exp: the f prefix turns on interpolation
start of a field
any expression: a name, arithmetic, a call
optional conversion: !r uses repr(), !s uses str()
starts the format spec
align: < left, > right, ^ centre, = pad after the sign
minimum width in characters
thousands separator (or _)
precision: digits after the point for floats, max length for strings
type: f fixed, e exponent, d integer, b binary, x hex, % percent, s string
end of the field
end of the literal

blocks.code:
rtt = 11.8421
port = 443
name = "router"
print(f"{name:<10}{rtt:>8.2f} ms")
print(f"{200:08b} {255:#x} {255:X} {10:02x} {1234567:,} {0.256:.1%}")
print(f"{port=} {name!r} {2 * port + 1}")
width = 12
print(f"[{name:^{width}}]")
for host, ms in [("gw", 1.2), ("dns", 14.75), ("far", 187.0)]:
    print(f"{host:<5}|{ms:>8.1f}|")

blocks.text: The `=` form (`{port=}`) prints the expression and its value, which makes it the best quick debugging aid. `{name:^{width}}` nests a field inside the spec so the width can be a variable. Older styles still work: `"%s is %d" % (name, 5)` and `"{} is {}".format(name, 5)`; you will meet them in other people's code.
Before Python 3.12 you could not reuse the same quote type inside an f-string expression: `f"{d["k"]}"` was a SyntaxError. Write `f"{d['k']}"` and it works on every version.
bytes and text encodings

Networks and files carry **bytes**: integers from 0 to 255. Text is a different thing: a sequence of characters. An **encoding** is the agreed mapping between them, and **UTF-8** is the one almost everything uses (ASCII text is identical in UTF-8; other characters take 2 to 4 bytes). Python keeps the two types strictly apart: `str` for text, `bytes` for raw data, and you convert explicitly.

blocks.code:
text = "héllo"
data = text.encode("utf-8")
print(data, len(text), len(data))
print(data.decode("utf-8"))
print(b"GET / HTTP/1.1\r\n"[:3], b"GET"[0], list(b"AB"))
print(bytes([71, 69, 84]), bytes.fromhex("c0a80101"), b"\xc0\xa8\x01\x01".hex())
print(int.from_bytes(b"\xc0\xa8\x01\x01", "big"), (3232235777).to_bytes(4, "big"))
print("naïve".encode("ascii", errors="replace"), b"A" == "A")
blocks.out:
b'h\xc3\xa9llo' 5 6
héllo
b'GET' 71 [65, 66]
b'GET' b'\xc0\xa8\x01\x01' c0a80101
3232235777 b'\xc0\xa8\x01\x01'
b'na?ve' False

blocks.text: Read the output closely. The 5-character word became 6 bytes because `é` takes two bytes in UTF-8. Indexing `bytes` gives an `int`, not a one-character `bytes`. `bytes([...])` builds bytes from integers, and `.hex()` and `bytes.fromhex()` convert to and from a hex string, which is exactly how you move between a packet dump and Python. The four bytes `c0 a8 01 01` are the address 192.168.1.1, and read as a big-endian integer they equal 3232235777. Big-endian ("network byte order") means the most significant byte comes first, as it does in every IP header.

blocks.title: Mixing str and bytes is an error on purpose

blocks.text: `b"abc" + "def"` raises `TypeError`, and `b"A" == "A"` is just `False`. Sockets send and receive bytes, so you will `.encode()` before sending and `.decode()` after receiving. Decoding bytes that are not valid in the chosen encoding raises `UnicodeDecodeError`; `errors="replace"` swaps bad bytes for a placeholder instead.
Operators

head: Group
Operators
Notes
rows: `+` and `*` also work on strings and lists
short-circuit and return one of their operands
work on the bits of integers
is this item inside this container or string?

blocks.text: Comparison and logic

Comparisons chain the way mathematics reads: `1 <= port <= 65535` means `1 <= port and port <= 65535`, with `port` evaluated once. `and` and `or` evaluate left to right and **stop as soon as the answer is known** (short-circuit). They return the deciding *operand*, not necessarily a `bool`, which gives Python its default-value idiom.

blocks.code:
port = 8080
print(1 <= port <= 65535, 1024 <= port < 8000)
print(False and print("never printed"))
print("" or "guest", "alice" or "guest", 0 or None, [] and 1, 1 and 2)
user = ""
name = user or "anonymous"
print(name)
print(not 0, not "x", "a" < "b", "Z" < "a", "10" < "9")
blocks.out:
True False
False
guest alice None [] 2
anonymous
True False True True True

blocks.text: The last line is a trap: strings compare **character by character** by code point, so `"10" < "9"` is `True` and uppercase sorts before lowercase. Convert to numbers when you mean numbers.
Bitwise operators and network masks
Bitwise operators treat an integer as a row of bits. They are how masks, flags and checksums work, and they are the reason IPv4 addresses are easiest to handle as 32-bit integers.

head: Operator
Name
Rule
Example
rows: bit is 1 only if both are 1

blocks.text: Python's `~` works on unlimited integers, so `~mask` is a negative number. Always mask the result with `& 0xFFFFFFFF` to keep 32 bits.

blocks.title: Apply a mask to an address

tokens.exp: result: the network address as a 32-bit integer
assignment
the address as an integer
bitwise AND: keep a bit only where both sides have a 1
32 bits with `prefix` ones followed by zeros

blocks.code:
parts = "192.168.1.10".split(".")
ip = (int(parts[0]) << 24) | (int(parts[1]) << 16) | (int(parts[2]) << 8) | int(parts[3])
prefix = 24
mask = (0xFFFFFFFF << (32 - prefix)) & 0xFFFFFFFF
network = ip & mask
wildcard = ~mask & 0xFFFFFFFF
broadcast = network | wildcard

def dotted(n):
    return ".".join(str((n >> shift) & 0xFF) for shift in (24, 16, 8, 0))

print(ip, hex(ip), f"{ip:032b}")
print("mask     ", dotted(mask))
print("network  ", dotted(network))
print("broadcast", dotted(broadcast))
print("hosts    ", broadcast - network - 1)

blocks.text: Flags work the same way. A TCP segment's flag byte packs one flag per bit, so you test one with `&` and set one with `|`:

blocks.code:
SYN, ACK, FIN = 0x02, 0x10, 0x01
flags = SYN | ACK
print(hex(flags), bool(flags & SYN), bool(flags & FIN))
flags &= ~SYN          # clear SYN
print(hex(flags), flags == ACK)
print(6 & 3 == 2)      # Python: & binds tighter than ==, so this is (6 & 3) == 2

blocks.text: In C, `==` binds tighter than `&`, so `x & 1 == 0` means something else there. In Python bitwise operators bind tighter than comparisons, so `x & 1 == 0` is `(x & 1) == 0`. Parentheses still make intent obvious, and they cost nothing.
Membership and identity
`in` asks whether an item is inside a container (or a substring inside a string). `is` asks whether two names point at the very same object, which is different from `==` (equal values).

blocks.code:
print("ssh" in "openssh", 22 in [22, 80], "ssh" not in ["http"])
a = [1, 2]
b = [1, 2]
c = a
print(a == b, a is b, a is c)
x = None
print(x is None, x is not None)
blocks.out:
True True True
True False True
True False

blocks.text: Use `==` for values and `is` only for `None`, `True` and `False`.
Precedence

When an expression mixes operators, Python applies them in this order, highest first. Operators on the same row group left to right (except the power operator, which groups right to left). Use parentheses whenever the reader would have to look this table up.

head: Priority
Operators
rows: conditional expression `a if c else b`, then `lambda`, then `:=`

blocks.text: Converting between types

Python never converts silently between text and numbers (`"5" + 5` is an error), so conversion is an explicit call: `int()`, `float()`, `str()`, `bool()`, `bytes()`. Each constructor accepts the types it understands and raises `ValueError` or `TypeError` when it cannot.

blocks.code:
print(int("42"), int(" 42\n"), int("ff", 16), int("0b101", 0), int("1_000"))
print(int(3.99), int(-3.99), float("1e3"), float("  2.5 "), str(3.0), str(None))
print(int(True), float(2), bool([]), list("abc"), tuple([1, 2]), str([1, 2]))

blocks.text: `int()` **truncates** toward zero (so `int(-3.99)` is `-3`); use `round`, `math.floor` or `math.ceil` when you want something else. Whitespace around a number is ignored. With base `0`, `int` reads the prefix (`0b`, `0o`, `0x`) to pick the base.
The most common error message in beginner Python is this one, and it is worth reading carefully:

blocks.code: print(int("3.5"))

blocks.text: The page shows `ValueError: invalid literal for int() with base 10: '3.5'`. It tells you the function (`int()`), the base it tried (10) and the offending text (`'3.5'`), so you can see exactly what was wrong. Convert in two steps when the text may hold a decimal: `int(float("3.5"))`.
Reading numbers safely from input

`input()` gives text, so the standard pattern converts straight away and decides what to do when the text is not a number. You will see the full `try`/`except` form in [Errors](#py-errors); the check below needs only a string method:
Names, references and mutability
In Python a variable is a **name** attached to an object, not a box holding a value. Assignment never copies the object; it attaches another name to it.

blocks.code:
a = [1, 2]            a ──┐
   b = a                     ├──▶  [1, 2]          one list, two names
                         b ──┘
   b.append(3)           a and b both show [1, 2, 3]

   c = a.copy()          c ───────▶  [1, 2, 3]     a second, independent list

blocks.text: Whether this matters depends on whether the object can change. **Immutable** objects (`int`, `float`, `bool`, `str`, `bytes`, `tuple`, `frozenset`, `None`) can never be modified, so sharing them is harmless. **Mutable** objects (`list`, `dict`, `set`, `bytearray`) can be modified in place, so every name sees the change.

blocks.code:
x = 5
y = x
y += 1                 # builds a new int and re-points y
print(x, y)
s = "net"
t = s
t += "work"            # builds a new str
print(s, t)
a = [1, 2]
b = a
b.append(3)            # modifies the one shared list
print(a, b, a is b)
print(id(x) == id(y), isinstance(a, list), isinstance(5, (int, float)))
blocks.out:
5 6
net network
[1, 2, 3] [1, 2, 3] True
False True True

blocks.text: Remember this picture; [Data structures](#py-data) returns to it with copying, default arguments and nested lists, where it causes most real bugs.
Built-in function reference

These functions are always available without importing anything. `print()`, `input()`, `help()`, `dir()`, `type()` and `id()` have cards in [Python start](#py-start). Each card here has a runnable example: press its Run button and change the arguments.

blocks.name: int()
blocks.sum: Convert a number or numeric text to an integer.

how.text: With a float, `int` truncates toward zero. With a string it parses the text in the given base (2 to 36, or 0 to read a `0x`/`0b`/`0o` prefix) and raises `ValueError` when the text is not a whole number.

examples.desc: Sum the fourth column (port) of users.csv, converting each text field
examples.code: cut -d, -f4 users.csv | tail -n +2 | python3 -c 'import sys; print(sum(int(x) for x in sys.stdin))'

blocks.name: float()
blocks.sum: Convert a number or numeric text to a floating-point number.

how.text: Parses decimal text including exponents (`1e3`), `inf` and `nan`, ignoring surrounding whitespace. Converting an `int` larger than about 1.8e308 raises `OverflowError`.

examples.desc: Average the RTT values in ping.log
examples.code: grep -o 'time=[0-9.]*' ping.log | cut -d= -f2 | python3 -c 'import sys; v = [float(x) for x in sys.stdin]; print(sum(v) / len(v))'

blocks.name: str()
blocks.sum: Return the printable text form of an object (or decode bytes with an encoding).
blocks.syntax: str(object='') -> str    str(bytes_or_buffer, encoding, errors) -> str

how.text: `str(x)` calls `x.__str__()`, the human-readable form. `str(b"abc", "utf-8")` decodes bytes, the same as `b"abc".decode("utf-8")`. Without an encoding, `str(b"abc")` returns the literal text `"b'abc'"`, which is almost never what you want.

examples.desc: Join the line lengths of ips.txt into one text value
examples.code: python3 -c 'import sys; print("-".join(str(len(l.strip())) for l in sys.stdin))' < ips.txt

gotchas: `str(b"hi")` without an encoding gives `"b'hi'"`. Always pass the encoding or use `.decode()`.

blocks.name: bool()
blocks.sum: Convert any value to True or False by Python's truthiness rules.

how.text: Returns `False` for the falsy values (zero, empty containers and strings, `None`) and `True` for everything else. Conditions call it implicitly, so `if items:` is the idiomatic way to ask "is the list non-empty?".

examples.code: print(bool(0), bool(""), bool([]), bool("0"), bool([0]), bool(None))
examples.out: False False False True True False

blocks.name: abs()
blocks.sum: Absolute value of a number (magnitude of a complex number).

how.text: Works on `int`, `float` and `complex`, and on any object that defines `__abs__`. It returns a value of the same kind (a float for a float).

examples.desc: Largest absolute difference between consecutive RTTs
examples.code: grep -o 'time=[0-9.]*' ping.log | cut -d= -f2 | python3 -c 'import sys; v = [float(x) for x in sys.stdin]; print(max(abs(a - b) for a, b in zip(v, v[1:])))'

blocks.name: round()
blocks.sum: Round a number to a given number of decimal digits.

how.text: With no `ndigits` it returns an `int`, rounding ties to the nearest even number (banker's rounding). With `ndigits` it returns a number of the same type, and negative values round to tens, hundreds and so on. Float representation can make `round(2.675, 2)` surprising (`2.67`).

examples.desc: Round the mean packet size to two decimals
examples.code: awk '{print $10}' access.log | python3 -c 'import sys; v = [int(x) for x in sys.stdin]; print(round(sum(v) / len(v), 2))'

blocks.name: min()
blocks.sum: Smallest item of an iterable, or of several arguments.
blocks.syntax: min(iterable, *, key=None, default=...)    min(a, b, *rest, key=None)

how.text: Compares items with `<`. The `key` function maps each item to the value to compare (`min(words, key=len)`), and `default` is returned for an empty iterable instead of raising `ValueError`. Ties return the first smallest item.

examples.desc: Smallest of several kinds of input
examples.code: print(min(4, 2, 9), min([3.5, 1.25]), min(["pi", "router", "nas"], key=len), min([], default=None))
grep -o 'time=[0-9.]*' ping.log | cut -d= -f2 | python3 -c 'import sys; print(min(float(x) for x in sys.stdin))'

blocks.name: max()
blocks.sum: Largest item of an iterable, or of several arguments.
blocks.syntax: max(iterable, *, key=None, default=...)    max(a, b, *rest, key=None)

how.text: The mirror image of `min`: same `key` and `default` parameters, first largest item wins ties. Strings compare by code point, so `max("a", "B")` is `"a"`.

examples.desc: Largest item and largest by key

examples.code: grep -o 'time=[0-9.]*' ping.log | cut -d= -f2 | python3 -c 'import sys; print(max(float(x) for x in sys.stdin))'

blocks.name: sum()
blocks.sum: Add up the items of an iterable, starting from a start value.

how.text: Adds left to right. It is meant for numbers; for joining strings use `"".join(...)`. For floats, `math.fsum` is more accurate because it tracks lost precision.

examples.code: print(sum([1, 2, 3]), sum([0.5, 0.25], 10), sum(x * x for x in range(4)))
awk '{print $10}' access.log | python3 -c 'import sys; print(sum(int(x) for x in sys.stdin))'

gotchas: `sum(["a", "b"])` raises `TypeError`; Python refuses on purpose because repeated string concatenation is slow.

blocks.name: pow()
blocks.sum: Raise a number to a power, optionally modulo a third number.

how.text: `pow(a, b)` equals `a ** b`. With three integer arguments it computes `a ** b % mod` efficiently without ever building the huge intermediate number, which is the core operation of modular arithmetic in cryptography.

blocks.name: divmod()
blocks.sum: Return the quotient and remainder of a division as a pair.

how.text: One call computes floor quotient and remainder together. It is the neat way to split seconds into minutes and seconds, or an index into a row and column.

examples.desc: Split a duration and a byte count
examples.code:
print(divmod(3725, 60), divmod(-7, 2))
hours, rest = divmod(3725, 3600)
minutes, seconds = divmod(rest, 60)
print(f"{hours}h {minutes}m {seconds}s")

examples.desc: Print uptime-like text from a number of seconds in a shell variable

blocks.name: len()
blocks.sum: Number of items in a container, characters in a string or bytes in a bytes object.

how.text: `len` asks the object how many items it holds. For `str` it counts characters, not bytes, so `len("é")` is 1 while `len("é".encode())` is 2. Generators and iterators have no length.

examples.code: print(len("router"), len([1, 2, 3]), len({"a": 1}), len(b"\xc0\xa8"), len("é"), len("é".encode()), len(range(10)))
python3 -c 'import sys; print(max(len(l.rstrip("\n")) for l in sys.stdin))' < notes.txt

gotchas: `len(5)` is a `TypeError`: numbers have no length. Convert with `len(str(5))` if you mean digits.

blocks.name: isinstance()
blocks.sum: Test whether an object is an instance of a class or any class in a tuple of classes.

how.text: Unlike `type(x) == T`, `isinstance` also accepts subclasses, so `isinstance(True, int)` is `True`. Pass a tuple to accept several types at once.

examples.code: print(isinstance(5, int), isinstance(5.0, int), isinstance(5, (int, float)), isinstance("5", str), isinstance(True, int))

blocks.name: bin()
blocks.sum: Return the binary text form of an integer, prefixed with 0b.

how.text: Works for negative integers too (`bin(-5)` is `'-0b101'`). Remove the prefix with a slice or use a format spec: `f"{x:b}"` and `f"{x:08b}"` give the digits only, padded.

examples.desc: Binary of numbers and a mask
Show each octet of an address in binary
examples.code: echo 192.168.1.10 | python3 -c 'import sys; print(*(f"{int(o):08b}" for o in input().split(".")), sep=".")'

blocks.name: hex()
blocks.sum: Return the hexadecimal text form of an integer, prefixed with 0x.

how.text: Digits are lowercase. For padded or uppercase output use `f"{x:02X}"`. `int(text, 16)` goes the other way and accepts the `0x` prefix.

examples.desc: Hex of numbers and from text
Print an IPv4 address as one hex value
examples.code: echo 192.168.1.10 | python3 -c 'print("0x" + "".join(f"{int(o):02x}" for o in input().split(".")))'

blocks.name: oct()
blocks.sum: Return the octal text form of an integer, prefixed with 0o.

how.text: Octal is rare outside Unix file modes, where each digit is three permission bits. `oct(0o755)` and `0o755` are the same number; `os.chmod(path, 0o755)` takes an octal literal.

examples.desc: Convert a numeric mode from the shell

blocks.name: ord()
blocks.sum: Return the Unicode code point (integer) of a one-character string.

how.text: For ASCII characters the result matches the ASCII table (`ord("A")` is 65). It accepts exactly one character; longer strings raise `TypeError`. `chr` is the inverse.

examples.code: print(ord("A"), ord("a"), ord("0"), ord("€"), [ord(c) for c in "GET"])

examples.desc: Print the codes of a word piped into Python
examples.code: echo -n HTTP | python3 -c 'import sys; print(*map(ord, sys.stdin.read()))'

blocks.name: chr()
blocks.sum: Return the one-character string for a Unicode code point.

how.text: Valid code points run from 0 to 0x10FFFF. Combine `chr` and `ord` for character arithmetic such as shifting letters in a Caesar cipher: `chr((ord(c) - 97 + 3) % 26 + 97)`.

examples.code:
print(chr(72) + chr(105), chr(0x20AC), "".join(chr(n) for n in [71, 69, 84]))
print(chr((ord("x") - 97 + 3) % 26 + 97))

examples.desc: Decode a space-separated list of ASCII codes
examples.code: echo 72 84 84 80 | python3 -c 'print("".join(chr(int(n)) for n in input().split()))'

blocks.name: repr()
blocks.sum: Return the unambiguous, developer-oriented text form of an object.

how.text: Where `str` aims at readers, `repr` aims at programmers: strings gain quotes, escapes are visible, and for many types `eval(repr(x))` would rebuild the object. The REPL and `{x!r}` in f-strings use it. It is the first tool to reach for when text contains invisible characters.

examples.code:
s = "ping \t ok\n"
print(s)
print(repr(s), str(s) == s, repr(3.0), repr(None))

examples.desc: Reveal stray whitespace and carriage returns in a file's lines
examples.code: python3 -c 'import sys; print(*(repr(l) for l in sys.stdin), sep="\n")' < hosts.txt | head -3

gotchas: When two strings look equal but compare unequal, print their `repr`: you will see a trailing space, tab or `\r`.

blocks.name: format()
blocks.sum: Format one value with a format spec: the same mini-language f-strings use after the colon.

how.text: `format(x, spec)` is what `f"{x:spec}"` calls. It is handy when the spec itself is computed, or in `map` and `sorted` pipelines where a lambda would be noisy.

examples.code:
print(format(3.14159, ".2f"), format(255, "08b"), format(1234567, ","), format("ip", ">6"))
spec = ">10.1f"
print(format(2.25, spec) + "|")

blocks.text: String method reference

A method is a function attached to a value and called with a dot: `"abc".upper()`. Strings are immutable, so **every method returns a new string** (or a list, number or bool) and leaves the original untouched. Forgetting to keep the result is a classic bug: `s.strip()` on its own line does nothing useful, while `s = s.strip()` does.
The cards run in the page and are grouped as: case, trimming, splitting and joining, searching, testing, padding and alignment, and encoding and translation.

tokens.exp: three names that receive the three parts
assignment unpacks the 3-tuple on the right
split at the first "=" into (before, "=", after); never raises

blocks.title: Join numbers into a dotted address

tokens.exp: the separator string, then its join method
a generator expression: convert each integer to text
end of the call; the result is one string such as "192.168.1.1"

blocks.name: str.upper()
blocks.sum: Return a copy with all letters in upper case.

how.text: Uses Unicode case mapping, so `"straße".upper()` is `"STRASSE"`. The original string is unchanged.

blocks.name: str.lower()
blocks.sum: Return a copy with all letters in lower case.

how.text: Normalise case before comparing or looking up keys: host names and HTTP header names are case-insensitive, so store them lower-cased. For caseless matching of international text prefer `casefold`.

blocks.name: str.title()
blocks.sum: Return a copy with the first letter of each word in upper case and the rest lower.

how.text: A "word" is any run of letters, so apostrophes and digits start new words. For sentence-style capitalisation use `capitalize`.

gotchas: `"they're".title()` gives `"They'Re"`. Do not use `title` for names with apostrophes.

blocks.name: str.capitalize()
blocks.sum: Return a copy with the first character upper-case and every other character lower-case.

how.text: Only the first character is upper-cased, and the rest is forced to lower case, so existing capitals are lost.

blocks.name: str.casefold()
blocks.sum: Return an aggressively lower-cased copy suited to caseless comparison.

how.text: Stronger than `lower`: it maps characters such as the German `ß` to `ss`, so `"Straße"` and `"STRASSE"` compare equal after folding.

blocks.name: str.swapcase()
blocks.sum: Return a copy with upper-case letters made lower-case and the reverse.

how.text: Rarely useful outside puzzles, but it shows that case operations are character by character.

blocks.name: str.strip()
blocks.sum: Return a copy without leading and trailing whitespace, or without any of the given characters.

how.text: With no argument it removes spaces, tabs and newlines from both ends. With `chars` it removes **any combination of those characters** from both ends, stopping at the first character not in the set. This is the call that cleans every line you read from a file or `input()`.

examples.desc: Strip each line and drop empty ones
examples.code:
printf '  a  

 b
' | python3 -c 'import sys; print(*(l.strip() for l in sys.stdin if l.strip()), sep="|")'

gotchas: The argument is a set of characters, not a prefix: `"https://sample".lstrip("https://")` returns `"ample"`. Use `removeprefix` for prefixes.

blocks.name: str.lstrip()
blocks.sum: Return a copy without leading whitespace (or leading characters from a set).

how.text: Like `strip` but only the left end. Same set-of-characters rule for the argument.

blocks.name: str.rstrip()
blocks.sum: Return a copy without trailing whitespace (or trailing characters from a set).

how.text: The usual way to remove the newline from a line read from a file: `line.rstrip("\n")` removes only the newline and keeps trailing spaces, while `rstrip()` removes all trailing whitespace.

examples.desc: Show lines with their trailing whitespace trimmed
examples.code: python3 -c 'import sys; print(*(l.rstrip() for l in sys.stdin), sep="\n")' < notes.txt | head -3

blocks.name: str.removeprefix()
blocks.sum: Return a copy without the given prefix, if the string starts with it (Python 3.9+).

how.text: Removes the exact prefix once, or returns the string unchanged if it does not start with it. This does what beginners expect `lstrip` to do.

blocks.name: str.removesuffix()
blocks.sum: Return a copy without the given suffix, if the string ends with it (Python 3.9+).

how.text: Exact and non-repeating. Use it to drop a file extension or a trailing dot from a DNS name.

examples.desc: Remove an extension and a root dot

blocks.name: str.split()
blocks.sum: Split a string into a list of substrings on a separator, or on runs of whitespace.

how.text: With no `sep`, it splits on any run of whitespace and discards empty strings at the ends, which mirrors how `awk` splits fields. With an explicit `sep`, every occurrence splits, so consecutive separators yield empty strings. `maxsplit` limits the number of splits.

examples.desc: Take field 1 of each line (the Python version of awk '{print $1}') and rank the clients
examples.code: python3 -c 'import sys; print(*(l.split()[0] for l in sys.stdin), sep="\n")' < access.log | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head -3

blocks.name: str.rsplit()
blocks.sum: Like split, but counting splits from the right.

how.text: Only differs from `split` when `maxsplit` is given. It is the right tool for peeling a file name or port off the end of a string.

blocks.name: str.splitlines()
blocks.sum: Split text at line boundaries and return the lines without their endings.

how.text:
Recognises `
`, `
` and `` (and some Unicode boundaries), so it handles files from any system. Unlike `split("
")` it does not produce an empty last element for a final newline.

examples.desc: Lines of a block of text

examples.code: python3 -c 'import sys; print(len([l for l in sys.stdin.read().splitlines() if l]))' < notes.txt

blocks.name: str.join()
blocks.sum: Concatenate the strings of an iterable, with the string as the separator between them.

how.text: Called on the *separator*, not on the list. It builds the result in one pass, so it is far faster than adding strings in a loop. Every item must be a `str`; convert numbers first.

examples.desc: Collapse the lines of ips.txt into one comma-separated line
examples.code: python3 -c 'import sys; print(",".join(l.strip() for l in sys.stdin))' < ips.txt

gotchas: `",".join([1, 2])` raises `TypeError: sequence item 0: expected str instance, int found`. Wrap in `str()`.

blocks.name: str.replace()
blocks.sum: Return a copy with every occurrence of a substring replaced by another.

how.text: Matches the exact text (no patterns; use `re.sub` for those). Scans left to right without overlapping. `count` limits how many replacements happen.

examples.desc: Replace the MAC separator across a stream

gotchas: The original is not changed. Write `s = s.replace(...)`.

blocks.name: str.find()
blocks.sum: Return the lowest index where a substring starts, or -1 if it is absent.

how.text: The -1 return is safe to test but dangerous to use as an index: `s[s.find("x")]` silently reads the last character when `find` returns -1. Use `in` for a pure yes/no question and `index` when absence is an error.

examples.code:
s = "GET /index.html HTTP/1.1"
print(s.find("/"), s.find("HTTP"), s.find("POST"), s.find("/", 5))

examples.desc: Show the position of the first 404 in each matching line
examples.code: python3 -c 'import sys; print(*(l.find(" 404 ") for l in sys.stdin if " 404 " in l))' < access.log

blocks.name: str.rfind()
blocks.sum: Return the highest index where a substring starts, or -1.

how.text: Searches from the right. Useful for the last dot in a file name or the last slash in a path.

blocks.name: str.index()
blocks.sum: Like find, but raise ValueError when the substring is missing.

how.text: Choose `index` when a missing substring means the data is malformed and you want the program to stop. `rindex` is the right-to-left twin.

examples.desc: Print the text before the first colon of each line
examples.code: printf 'Host: a\nUser: b\n' | python3 -c 'import sys; print(*(l[:l.index(":")] for l in sys.stdin))'

blocks.name: str.count()
blocks.sum: Count non-overlapping occurrences of a substring.

how.text: Counting is left to right and non-overlapping: `"aaaa".count("aa")` is 2. Count single characters to check structure, for example that an IPv4 string has three dots.

examples.desc: Count lines mentioning ERROR in notes.txt

blocks.name: str.startswith()
blocks.sum: Test whether the string begins with a prefix, or with any prefix in a tuple.

how.text: Pass a tuple to test several prefixes at once. It is more readable and faster than slicing and comparing.

examples.desc: Keep only the private 10.x lines of ips.txt
examples.code: python3 -c 'import sys; print(*(l.strip() for l in sys.stdin if l.startswith("10.")), sep="\n")' < ips.txt

blocks.name: str.endswith()
blocks.sum: Test whether the string ends with a suffix, or with any suffix in a tuple.

how.text: The usual file-type test. Remember that it is case sensitive, so lower the name first when matching extensions.

examples.desc: Show only the .log names from a listing
examples.code: ls ~/lab | python3 -c 'import sys; print(*(l.strip() for l in sys.stdin if l.endswith(".log\n")), sep="\n")'

blocks.name: str.isdigit()
blocks.sum: True if every character is a digit and the string is not empty.

how.text: Also accepts superscript digits such as `²`, which `int()` cannot convert. For plain 0 to 9 use `isdecimal`, or just try `int()`. Signs, spaces and decimal points are not digits: `"-5".isdigit()` and `"3.5".isdigit()` are both `False`.

examples.code:
printf '22
ssh
443
' | python3 -c 'import sys; print(*(l.strip() for l in sys.stdin if l.strip().isdigit()))'

blocks.name: str.isdecimal()
blocks.sum: True if every character is a decimal digit (a character that can form a base-10 number) and the string is not empty.

how.text: The strictest digit test: it accepts exactly what `int()` accepts as digits (including non-ASCII decimal digits such as Arabic-Indic numerals) and rejects `²`. `isnumeric` is the loosest and also accepts fractions like `½`.

blocks.name: str.isalpha()
blocks.sum: True if every character is a letter and the string is not empty.

how.text: Letters from any alphabet count, so `"héllo".isalpha()` is `True`. Spaces, digits and punctuation do not.

blocks.name: str.isalnum()
blocks.sum: True if every character is a letter or a digit and the string is not empty.

how.text: A quick sanity check for identifiers and tokens that must contain no punctuation or spaces. Note the underscore is not alphanumeric.

blocks.name: str.isspace()
blocks.sum: True if the string is not empty and contains only whitespace.

how.text: Whitespace includes space, tab, newline, carriage return and some Unicode spaces. `"".isspace()` is `False`, so it is not the same as `not s`.

examples.desc: Count blank or whitespace-only lines from a stream
examples.code:
printf 'a

  
b
' | python3 -c 'import sys; print(sum(1 for l in sys.stdin if l.isspace()))'

blocks.name: str.isupper()
blocks.sum: True if the string has at least one cased letter and all its cased letters are upper-case.

how.text: Characters that have no case (digits, punctuation) are ignored, but at least one letter must be present.

blocks.name: str.islower()
blocks.sum: True if the string has at least one cased letter and all its cased letters are lower-case.

how.text: Mirror of `isupper`: digits and punctuation do not disqualify the string, but a string without any letter returns `False`.

blocks.name: str.isidentifier()
blocks.sum: True if the string is a valid Python name.

how.text: Checks letters, digits and underscores, with no leading digit. It does not check for reserved words; `"for".isidentifier()` is `True`, use `keyword.iskeyword` for that.

blocks.name: str.isascii()
blocks.sum: True if every character is in the 7-bit ASCII range (also true for the empty string).

how.text: A fast check before encoding as ASCII or before sending text to a protocol that only allows ASCII, such as classic email headers and DNS names.

blocks.name: str.zfill()
blocks.sum: Pad a numeric string on the left with zeros to a minimum width, keeping any sign in front.

how.text: Only pads; never truncates. Equivalent to the format spec `:0{width}` for numbers, but works on strings that are already text.

examples.desc: Pad sequence numbers from a stream to three digits
examples.code: seq 1 3 | python3 -c 'import sys; print(*(l.strip().zfill(3) for l in sys.stdin))'

blocks.name: str.center()
blocks.sum: Centre the string in a field of a given width, padding with a fill character.

how.text: When the padding is odd the extra character goes on the right. Returns the original string if it is already wider than `width`.

blocks.name: str.ljust()
blocks.sum: Left-align the string in a field of a given width, padding on the right.

how.text: The text-table workhorse: pad every first column to the width of the longest entry and the columns line up.

examples.code:
hosts = ["gw", "nas", "printer"]
w = max(len(h) for h in hosts)
for h in hosts:
    print(h.ljust(w), "|")

examples.desc: Align the first column of users.csv for reading
examples.code: python3 -c 'import sys; print(*(l.split(",")[0].ljust(8) + l.split(",")[1].strip() for l in sys.stdin), sep="\n")' < users.csv | head -4

blocks.name: str.rjust()
blocks.sum: Right-align the string in a field of a given width, padding on the left.

how.text: Use it for numbers so digits line up by place value. `str(n).rjust(6)` or the spec `f"{n:>6}"` do the same thing.

blocks.name: str.expandtabs()
blocks.sum: Replace tab characters with spaces up to the next tab stop.

how.text: Tab stops are columns that are multiples of `tabsize`, so a tab can become anywhere from one to `tabsize` spaces depending on its column. This is how terminals align tab-separated output.

examples.desc: Expand tabs in a stream so columns line up in any viewer

blocks.name: str.partition()
blocks.sum: Split at the first occurrence of a separator into a 3-tuple: before, separator, after.

how.text: Always returns three items. If the separator is absent you get `(s, "", "")`, so it never raises, which makes it ideal for `key=value` and `host:port` parsing.

examples.desc: Parse key=value and a missing separator
examples.code:
print("mode=fast=yes".partition("="))
key, sep, value = "nosep".partition("=")
print(repr(key), repr(sep), repr(value))

examples.desc: Print the value of each header-like line
examples.code:
printf 'Host: example.com
Accept: */*
' | python3 -c 'import sys; print(*(l.partition(": ")[2].strip() for l in sys.stdin), sep="
")'

blocks.name: str.rpartition()
blocks.sum: Split at the last occurrence of a separator into a 3-tuple.

how.text: Like `partition` but searching from the right. If the separator is missing you get `("", "", s)`.

blocks.name: str.encode()
blocks.sum: Encode the string to bytes using an encoding (UTF-8 by default).

how.text: Converts characters to bytes. `errors` chooses what happens to characters the encoding cannot represent: `strict` raises `UnicodeEncodeError`, `replace` uses `?`, `ignore` drops them, `backslashreplace` writes an escape.

examples.desc: Show the UTF-8 bytes of a piped word as hex

blocks.name: str.format()
blocks.sum: Substitute values into {} fields in a template string.

how.text: The pre-f-string formatting method. Fields can be positional (`{0}`), automatic (`{}`) or named (`{host}`) and take the same `:spec` as f-strings. Its advantage is that the template can live in a variable or a file and be filled in later.

blocks.name: str.format_map()
blocks.sum: Like format, but takes a single mapping (such as a dict) instead of keyword arguments.

how.text: The mapping is used directly, so `format_map(row)` fills a template from a dictionary without unpacking it, and a `dict` subclass can supply defaults for missing keys.

examples.desc: Fill a template from a record

blocks.name: str.translate()
blocks.sum: Replace or delete characters using a translation table.

how.text: The table maps code points to replacement strings, code points or `None` (delete). Build it with `str.maketrans`. It handles a whole set of single-character substitutions in one pass, which is faster than chained `replace` calls.

examples.desc: Strip separators from a MAC address and rot-style substitution
Delete all digits from a stream

blocks.name: str.maketrans()
blocks.sum: Build a translation table for translate, from two strings, a dict, or two strings plus characters to delete.

how.text: `maketrans("abc", "xyz")` pairs characters by position. A single dict maps characters (or code points) to replacements. A third string lists characters to delete. It is a static method, called on `str` itself.

blocks.text: Common mistakes

items.text: **Dropping the result of a string method.** `line.strip()` alone does nothing; assign it: `line = line.strip()`.
**Comparing text to numbers.** `"10" < "9"` is `True` and `"5" == 5` is `False`. Convert first.
**Using `==` with floats.** Use `math.isclose` or compare rounded values.
**`is` instead of `==`.** `x is 5` may work by accident for small ints and fail elsewhere. Use `==`.
**Expecting `input()` to give a number.** It gives a string, always.
**Integer division surprises.** `/` returns a float even for `6 / 3` (`2.0`); use `//` for a whole number.
**Mixing `str` and `bytes`.** Encode before sending, decode after receiving.
**Forgetting that `-` in a slice goes from the end.** `s[-3:]` is the last three characters, `s[:-3]` is everything except them.

blocks.text: Practice

blocks.title: Apply a prefix to an address

task.text: Write `network_address(ip, prefix)` that takes an IPv4 address string and a prefix length and returns the network address as a dotted string, using **bitwise operators** on the 32-bit integer form (no `ipaddress` module). For example `network_address("192.168.1.130", 25)` is `"192.168.1.128"`.

hints: Convert the four octets to one integer with shifts: `(a << 24) | (b << 16) | (c << 8) | d`.
The mask is `(0xFFFFFFFF << (32 - prefix)) & 0xFFFFFFFF`. Convert the result back with `(n >> shift) & 0xFF` for shift in 24, 16, 8, 0.

why.text: The mask has `prefix` leading ones. `& mask` keeps the network bits and clears the host bits. The final `& 0xFFFFFFFF` matters for `/0`, where the shift would otherwise leave extra high bits.

blocks.title: Parse key=value pairs

task.text: Write `parse_pairs(text)` that turns `"host=pi.lan;port=22;mode=fast"` into the dictionary `{"host": "pi.lan", "port": "22", "mode": "fast"}`. Ignore empty segments (a trailing semicolon) and strip spaces around keys and values. A segment without `=` should be skipped.

hints: `text.split(";")` gives the segments. Skip a segment when it is empty or has no `=`.
`segment.partition("=")` returns `(key, sep, value)` and `sep` is empty when `=` is absent. Build the dict with `result[key.strip()] = value.strip()`.

why.text: `partition` splits at the first `=` only, so values may contain `=`, and its empty separator tells you cheaply when a segment has none. Dictionaries are covered fully in the next chapters; here `result[key] = value` simply stores a pair.

blocks.check:
assert parse_pairs("host=pi.lan;port=22;mode=fast") == {"host": "pi.lan", "port": "22", "mode": "fast"}, "basic parse"
assert parse_pairs("a=1;;b = 2 ;") == {"a": "1", "b": "2"}, "empty segments and spaces"
assert parse_pairs("x=1=2;junk;y=") == {"x": "1=2", "y": ""}, "split only on the first = and skip junk"
assert parse_pairs("") == {}, "empty input"

blocks.title: Format a host table

task.text: Write `table(rows)` where `rows` is a list of `(host, rtt_ms)` pairs. Return one string with one line per row: the host left-aligned in 8 characters, then the RTT right-aligned in 8 characters with one decimal place, then ` ms`. Lines are joined with `\n` (no trailing newline). For `[("gw", 1.234), ("example", 12.5)]` the result is `"gw           1.2 ms\nexample     12.5 ms"`.

hints: Build a list of lines and use `"\n".join(lines)`.

why.text: Format specs do the alignment, so no manual padding is needed. Joining at the end avoids a trailing newline, and an empty list naturally yields an empty string.

blocks.check:
assert table([("gw", 1.234), ("example", 12.5)]) == "gw           1.2 ms\nexample     12.5 ms", "check widths: host 8 left, rtt 8 right, 1 decimal"
assert table([]) == "", "no rows -> empty string"
assert table([("a", 100)]) == "a          100.0 ms", "ints format as floats with :.1f"

blocks.title: Normalise a MAC address

task.text: Write `normalize_mac(text)` that accepts a MAC address written with `:`, `-` or `.` separators (or none) in any case, such as `"AA-bb-CC-dd-EE-ff"` or `"aabb.ccdd.eeff"`, and returns it as lower-case colon-separated pairs: `"aa:bb:cc:dd:ee:ff"`. Return `None` if the cleaned text is not exactly 12 hexadecimal digits.

hints: Remove the separators with `translate` or `replace`, lower-case the text, then check `len(...) == 12`.
Hex digits are `0123456789abcdef`; test every character with `all(c in "0123456789abcdef" for c in clean)` or use `int(clean, 16)` inside a check on the length.

why.text: `translate` with a delete-set removes every separator in one pass, slices of width 2 cut the pairs, and `join` reassembles them. Validating before formatting means bad input returns `None` instead of a half-formatted result.

blocks.check:
assert normalize_mac("AA-bb-CC-dd-EE-ff") == "aa:bb:cc:dd:ee:ff", "dashes"
assert normalize_mac("aabb.ccdd.eeff") == "aa:bb:cc:dd:ee:ff", "dotted groups"
assert normalize_mac("AABBCCDDEEFF") == "aa:bb:cc:dd:ee:ff", "no separators"
assert normalize_mac("aa:bb:cc") is None, "too short"
assert normalize_mac("zz:bb:cc:dd:ee:ff") is None, "not hex"

blocks.title: Break it on purpose: string addition

task.text: This program should print `Total: 30 ms`, but it prints the wrong thing. Run it, work out why, and fix **two** things: the types being added, and the output so it matches exactly.

why.text: This starter does not crash but prints `Total: 1020`, because `+` on strings joins them. That is the other half of the lesson: the dangerous bugs are the ones that do not raise. Converting with `int()` makes `+` mean addition, and a third argument to `print` adds the unit.

blocks.check: assert out.strip() == "Total: 30 ms", "expected 'Total: 30 ms' but got " + repr(out.strip())

questions.why: `//` rounds toward negative infinity, so -3.5 becomes -4. Truncation toward zero would give -3, which is what `int(-7 / 2)` returns.
Python rounds ties to the nearest even number (banker's rounding), so 2.5 becomes 2 and 3.5 becomes 4.

questions.q: Which line keeps the network bits of an address `ip` (as an integer) for a mask `mask`?
questions.why: AND keeps a bit only where the mask has a 1, which clears the host bits.

options.text: True, because strings compare character by character and "1" comes before "9"

questions.why: Text comparison is lexicographic by code point. Convert to `int` first when you mean numbers.
With an explicit separator every occurrence splits, so consecutive commas produce an empty string. Only `split()` with no argument discards empty pieces.

questions.q: How many bytes does the string "é" occupy in UTF-8?
questions.why: `é` is code point U+00E9, which UTF-8 encodes in two bytes (`c3 a9`). That is why `len("é")` is 1 but `len("é".encode())` is 2.

blocks.text: Next: [Control flow and functions](#py-flow) turns these values into programs: decisions, loops and reusable functions.

terms.def: Python's whole-number type; it has no size limit
The rule that decides whether a value counts as True or False in a condition
A piece of a sequence selected with start:stop:step, such as s[1:4]
A string literal prefixed with f whose {} fields are replaced by expression values
A rule for turning characters into bytes; UTF-8 is the standard one
An immutable sequence of integers from 0 to 255; the type of raw network data
Cannot be changed after creation (int, str, tuple); operations return new objects
An operator (& | ^ ~ << >>) that works on the individual bits of integers
Stopping the evaluation of and/or as soon as the result is known
A name pointing at an object; assignment copies the reference, not the object
